'''''Rhododendron groenlandicum''''' (formerly '''''Ledum groenlandicum''''' or '''''Ledum latifolium'''''<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kron | first1 = Kathleen Anne | last2 = Judd | year = 1990 | title =  Phylogenetic Relationships within the Rhodoreae (Ericaceae) with Specific Comments on the Placement of ''Ledum''| journal = [[Systematic Botany]] | volume = 15 | issue = 1| page = 67 | doi = 10.2307/2419016 | jstor = 2419016 | bibcode = 1990SysBo..15...57K }}</ref>), known by the common names '''bog Labrador tea''', '''muskeg tea''', '''swamp tea''', in northern Canada, '''Hudson's Bay tea''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=502}}</ref> and in Greenlandic, '''Qajaasaq''' ({{IPA|kl|qajaːsɑq|IPA}}, resembling a [[Kayak]]), is a species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[shrub]] in the family [[Ericaceae]]. Found in northern parts of North America and Greenland,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Perry |first1=Anne |last2=Levine |first2=Carol |date=1997 |title=A Guide to Wildflowers in Winter: Herbaceous Plants of Northeastern North America |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/3858412 |journal=Northeastern Naturalist |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=115 |doi=10.2307/3858412 |jstor=3858412 |issn=1092-6194|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  ''R. groenlandicum'' grows primarily in bogs and other wetlands, which tend to be also in cold, acidic, and nutrient-poor environments. It has traditionally been used to make medicinal herbal teas among the [[Dene]], [[Athabaskan languages|Athabaskan]], and [[Inuit]], and other indigenous cultures of North America peoples.

==Description==
It is a low [[shrub]] growing to {{cvt|50|cm|in|0}} tall – rarely up to {{cvt|2|m|ftin}} – with [[evergreen]] [[leaves]] {{cvt|2|–|6|cm|in|frac=8}} long and {{cvt|3|–|15|mm|in|frac=8}} broad. The leaves are wrinkled on top with a thick waxy cuticle and have a leathery texture. The underside is covered in dense white hair that turns red-brown with age. The flowers of ''R. groenlandicum'' are small, white, and perfect ([[Plant reproductive morphology|bisexual]]).<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Hébert |first1=François |last2=Thiffault |first2=Nelson |date=July 2011 |title=The Biology of Canadian Weeds. 146.''Rhododendron groenlandicum''(Oeder) Kron and Judd |url=https://doi.org/10.4141/cjps2010-012 |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=91 |issue=4 |pages=725–738 |doi=10.4141/cjps2010-012 |bibcode=2011CJPlS..91..725H |issn=0008-4220}}</ref> Their hemispherical clusters have up to 35 flowers with petals approximately 1 cm long. With 5 oval shaped petals it produces a sweet aroma and sticky nectar to attract pollinators.<ref name=":1" />

''R. groenlandicum'' is self-compatible; however, self-fertilization results in a lower fruit set and fewer seeds per fruit "than cross-pollination". Pollination is primarily performed by bees; however, butterflies and beetles can also act as pollinators.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/gao/9781884446054.article.t046369 |title=Kew, Royal Botanic Gardens of |date=2003 |publisher=Oxford University Press |series=Oxford Art Online |doi=10.1093/gao/9781884446054.article.t046369 }}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Ledum groenlandicum 018.jpg|thumb|[[Côte-Nord]], [[Quebec]], Canada]]
It is reported from [[Greenland]], as well as from every province and territory in [[Canada]] and in the northern [[United States]] including the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] ([[New England]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Pennsylvania]]), the [[Pacific Northwest|Northwest]] ([[Oregon]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], [[Idaho]], [[Alaska]]), and parts of the [[Upper Midwest]] ([[Michigan]], [[Wisconsin]], [[Minnesota]]).<ref>{{cite POWO|id=284230-2|title=''Rhododendron groenlandicum''|accessdate=27 March 2022}}</ref> It grows in bogs, [[muskeg]]s, and open tundra, as well as occasionally on wet shores and rocky alpine slopes.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250065635|title=''Rhododendron groenlandicum''|publisher=[[Flora of North America]]|journal=Systematic Botany|volume=15|issue=1|pages=57–68|year=1990|doi=10.2307/2419016|jstor=2419016|last1=Kron|first1=Kathleen A.|last2=Judd|first2=Walter S.|bibcode=1990SysBo..15...57K |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://plants.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/cs_legr.pdf|title=Plant Guide for bog Labrador tea (Ledum groenlandicum).|last=Anderson|first=M.|publisher=USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, National Plant Data Team.|year=2011|location=Greensboro, NC.}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
The plant contains toxic [[alkaloid]]s which are poisonous to livestock and may be toxic to humans in concentrated doses.<ref name=":0" />

== Harvesting ==
Due to the plant's slow growth, tea leaves are collected in the spring by taking only one leaf from each of multiple plants. Labrador tea is slow-growing, so only a single new leaf is collected from a plant every other year to avoid damaging the plants.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

== Uses ==
{{See also|Labrador tea}}
The leaves are regularly used to make beverages and medicines—most commonly a fragrant tea—by many Native American tribes such as the [[Quinault people|Quinault]] and [[Makah]], the [[Potawatomi]], the [[Anishinaabe]], the [[Iroquois]], and [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]] tribes in Canada.<ref name=":0" /> [[Antioxidant]], [[anti-inflammatory]] and [[anticancer]] activity has been found.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dufour |first1=Dominic |last2=Pichette |first2=André |last3=Mshvildadze |first3=Vakhtang |last4=Bradette-Hébert |first4=Marie-Eve |last5=Lavoie |first5=Serge |last6=Longtin |first6=Angélique |last7=Laprise |first7=Catherine |last8=Legault |first8=Jean |title=Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anticancer activities of methanolic extracts from Ledum groenlandicum Retzius |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=April 2007 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=22–28 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2006.10.021 |pmid=17156957 }}</ref> When European explorers arrived, they soon adopted these uses as well, dubbing it "Indian plant tea".<ref name=":0" /> During the [[American Revolutionary War]], it was used as a substitute for tea.<ref name=":0" /> It was used as ale flavoring in Europe prior to [[hops]] becoming the main flavoring and [[preservative]] ingredient.<ref>Susan Verberg, The Rise and Fall of Gruit, Copyright © Susan Verberg, 2018.</ref><ref>Richard W. Unger, Beer in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, 2004 University of Pennsylvania Press, p31-2</ref>

''Rhododendron groenlandicum'' is sometimes grown as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental shrub]].<ref name=":0" /> Its [[essential oil]] is also popular in [[aromatherapy]].<ref name=":0" />
